title: Bedbugs: care for bites and stop the infestation
intro: Bedbugs are insects that hide near sleeping places and feed on blood. Finding them can be upsetting, but an infestation does not mean a home is dirty. There are two separate tasks: relieving any skin reaction and removing the insects. Treating the itching alone will not stop further bites, while indiscriminate spraying can create additional health risks.

sections.heading: Check the room rather than diagnosing from a rash
paragraphs: Itchy raised marks after sleep can suggest bites, but their appearance cannot reliably identify bedbugs. Fleas, mosquitoes, eczema and other problems can look similar. People sharing a bed may react differently, and some have no visible marks. Look for insects, shed skins or dark spotting around mattress seams and bed frames. A photograph or a safely contained specimen can help a pest professional identify the problem. Avoid carrying potentially infested bedding through other rooms uncovered.

sections.heading: Relieve symptoms without damaging the skin
paragraphs: Gently clean affected skin and use a cool compress for discomfort. Scratching can break the skin and increase infection risk. A pharmacist can advise whether an anti-itch treatment is suitable, taking account of age, pregnancy, other medicines and the area affected. Never apply household insecticide, disinfectant or an animal flea product to your skin. Persistent itching without evidence of an infestation deserves a medical assessment rather than repeated pesticide treatment.

sections.heading: Recognise when a skin problem needs medical help
paragraphs: Seek medical advice for increasing pain, warmth, swelling, pus or spreading redness, particularly with fever or feeling unwell. Colour changes may be less obvious on darker skin, so pay attention to tenderness and heat too. Breathing difficulty, swelling of the mouth or throat, or collapse requires emergency help. Bedbugs are not known to transmit human disease, but allergic reactions, infected scratches and disrupted sleep can still require care.

sections.heading: Arrange a coordinated pest-control plan
paragraphs: Contact a qualified pest-control service and, where relevant, the landlord or accommodation manager. Explain which rooms are affected and whether children, pregnant people or pets are present. Treatment often combines inspection, carefully chosen physical measures and appropriate insecticides, with repeat checks. Follow instructions about bagging, laundering, drying and re-entering treated rooms. Do not mix chemicals, use outdoor pesticides indoors or attempt to heat a room with improvised heaters. These methods can cause poisoning or fire.

sections.heading: Reduce spread and check whether treatment worked
paragraphs: Moving bedding or furniture to another room can move the insects too. Ask the pest specialist what to keep, clean or discard; throwing everything away is not automatically necessary. Inspect second-hand furniture before bringing it home and check luggage after a suspected exposure. Keep a record of sightings and treatment dates. New itching alone is not proof that treatment failed because skin reactions can be delayed. Continued sightings need follow-up with the service, and ongoing sleep loss or anxiety deserves support.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: bites after travel
examples.text: After returning from a trip, a person notices itchy marks. Instead of spraying the whole bedroom, they photograph a small insect found in a mattress seam, contain the luggage and ask a pest service to identify it. A pharmacist separately advises on the itching.

examples.title: Hypothetical example: worsening skin symptoms
examples.text: A resident scratches a bite until it bleeds. The next day the area becomes hot, painful and increasingly swollen. They seek medical assessment for possible infection while the building manager coordinates inspection of the affected rooms.

questions: Could these skin changes have another cause, and which signs suggest infection?
Which itch treatment is suitable for my age, medicines and skin?
